comparison: Use the uniform finite average of the environment-specific population second-moment matrices with denominator the number of environments. This is not sample-size weighting and not an empirical covariance estimate. Nonempty finite E is required for the intended averaging interpretation; totalized division at zero must not define an empty-environment model. Matrix addition and scalar multiplication form the average directly, and the previously stated common Loewner bounds are preserved by averaging the corresponding positive-semidefinite differences. The separate centering convention remains the reason these raw second moments are called covariances. Condition 4.3 uses the inverse square root of THIS pooled matrix in every environment, not an environment-specific whitening matrix; the averaging definition itself contains no inverse operation.
gap: Finite matrix averaging expresses the pooled covariance, with the intended nonempty environment domain and uniform weights retained.

Averaging preserves the shared quadratic-form bounds by ordinary finite-sum arithmetic; the source does not use sample-size weights or environment-specific whitening here.

comparison: Represent potential outcomes by a treatment-indexed family of real random variables a ↦ Y^a on a common probability space, preserving the continuous treatment-support domain. Measurable supplies the ordinary random-variable predicate for each member; this is a representation, not a library theorem identifying causal and observed quantities. This sentence does not identify Y^a with the observed Y, assert independence from A, specify distributions or give finite expectations. Joint measurability in treatment and sample point is a separate condition if evaluating the family at random A; measurability of each fixed-a member alone is not enough. Do not introduce a binary treatment model, an outcome-generating structural equation or a treatment smoothness condition solely from this definition.
gap: A treatment-indexed measurable family represents the potential outcomes; their causal identification and random-treatment evaluation need the separate source conditions.

The generic predicate encodes random variables but supplies neither causal identification nor joint measurability of an uncountable parameterized family.

comparison: Define theta_0(a) as the expectation of the potential outcome Y^a under the common population law, with integrability wherever the real-valued estimand is used. H_0 asserts existence of one real c with theta_0(a)=c over the stated treatment domain; H_1 is nonconstancy of that function, not a comparison to a prespecified c or to the observed conditional mean E(Y|A=a). The Bochner integral provides the expectation once integrability holds; its zero value for nonintegrable functions must not create a spurious constant null. The quoted sentence only announces later smoothness assumptions under nonconstancy, so do not choose a differentiability order here. comparison: Retain the structural consistency relation A=a implies Y=Y^a, using the same treatment-indexed family and observation on a common probability space. It is not convergence or consistency of a statistical estimator and does not assert that Y equals every potential outcome regardless of treatment. A measurable family can support the evaluation Y^{A(omega)}(omega), but fixed-a measurability alone does not establish that this diagonal evaluation is measurable. Also, for a continuous treatment, a separate almost-everywhere implication on each null event {A=a} can be vacuous; do not replace the source consistency relation by those pointwise-in-a probability-one statements and then infer equality at random A. Preserve the intended structural relation and state any common-version/joint-measurability requirement when formalizing it, rather than claiming the generic measurability predicate proves it.
gap: Ordinary function equality expresses consistency; a source-compatible common version is required when evaluating the potential-outcome family at the realized treatment.

comparison: For each fixed treatment level a, condition the integrable potential outcome Y^a on the sigma-algebra generated by (L,A), and equate that conditional mean with the conditional mean given L alone. comap supplies the two generated sigma-algebras for measurable covariates/treatment, and condExp supplies versions of the conditional expectations under their proper sub-sigma-algebra and integrability hypotheses. On a probability space the trimmed finite measure meets the required sigma-finiteness once those sigma-algebras are valid. Do not use the conditional-expectation fallback zero to satisfy the equality outside this domain. This is mean ignorability, not equality of conditional distributions or conditional independence of Y^a and A given L. Conditional expectations are identified almost everywhere; no pointwise identity for every l,a or a common null set over all uncountably many treatment levels follows without additional version arguments.
gap: Conditional expectation and generated sigma-algebras express mean ignorability, with integrability and the appropriate almost-everywhere version conditions retained.
